opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that once you have a system that's roughly at human level across a broad range of tasks, you no longer have a single human-level researcher. You have something you can copy thousands or millions of times, run faster than real time, and point at the problem of improving AI itself. So the bottleneck that has defined progress so far, the number of capable people working on the problem and how fast they can think and run experiments, suddenly loosens dramatically.

The second part, which ties into my own work on open-endedness, is that human data is a finite resource. Today we largely learn from the internet, which caps you somewhere around the distribution of human knowledge. But we've seen in narrower domains, like AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and more recently in reasoning and code, that once a system can generate its own data, propose its own problems, try things, and get feedback, it can go well beyond human performance. Those systems didn't stall at human level. They passed it, and then human level turned out to be just one point on the curve.

So if you combine a system that's generally capable enough to set its own goals, generate its own curriculum, and learn from interacting with the world or with simulations, with the ability to scale that massively in parallel, I don't see a natural reason for it to plateau at the human level. Human level isn't a special barrier from the system's point of view. It's a barrier from ours, because it's where our data runs out.

There are real caveats. Some progress needs the physical world: running experiments, building hardware, collecting new observations. That doesn't scale as easily as compute, and it could slow things down in certain domains. But in areas that are mostly digital, like math, software, and much of AI research itself, I'd expect the gap between "as good as a strong human" and "clearly beyond any human" to be much shorter than the path we took to get to human level in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level AI could be copied at scale, run faster, and directed to improve AI itself, loosening the research bottleneck and making the jump to superhuman capability much shorter.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key point is that once you have a system that's at human level across the board, you've essentially removed the bottleneck that has always constrained scientific progress, which is the number of capable researchers and the speed at which they can work. Human researchers need to sleep, they need years of training, they can only read so many papers, and knowledge transfer between them is slow and lossy. An AI system at that level doesn't have any of those limitations. You can run thousands of copies in parallel, they can share what they've learned directly, and they work around the clock.

And the crucial thing is that one of the problems these systems can work on is AI research itself. So you get this recursive dynamic where the system improves the methods that produce the next system, and that loop closes much faster than anything we've seen with humans in the loop. We're already seeing early versions of this with automated discovery of algorithms, of architectures, of training recipes, and in open-ended learning settings where the system generates its own curriculum of problems to solve. Right now humans are still very much the bottleneck in that loop, but once they aren't, I don't see why the pace would stay at human speed.

The other thing I'd say is that "human-level" isn't really a natural plateau. It's a point we care about because it's us, but there's nothing special about it from the perspective of the underlying capabilities. The systems are already superhuman in narrow ways, in memory, in breadth of knowledge, in speed. So the moment they're also human-level at the things they're currently weak at, things like long-horizon planning or genuine novelty, you don't get a human. You get something that's human-level at its weakest and far beyond that everywhere else. That combination, plus the ability to self-improve and scale, is why I think the jump happens fast rather than gradually.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level AI can conduct AI research and improve the methods that produce the next system, creating a fast recursive loop; it also describes running many copies in parallel and scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that human intelligence isn’t some natural ceiling. It’s a particular point on a spectrum, shaped by the constraints of biological evolution. There’s no obvious reason an artificial system would reach that point and then stop improving.

And once you have a system that can do research at roughly the level of a human researcher, it can contribute to improving AI itself. You can potentially run many copies of it, have them explore different ideas, and share what they learn. That creates a feedback loop: better AI helps us build even better AI.

That doesn’t mean the transition is guaranteed to be instantaneous. There are still constraints around compute, experiments, and how quickly you can validate new ideas. But human-level intelligence could be the point where the process accelerates, rather than the endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level AI could contribute to improving AI, with many copies exploring ideas and sharing results to create a feedback loop toward better AI. It also acknowledges compute constraints, which conveys the criterion’s sufficient-compute condition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that human intelligence is constrained by biology. We can’t simply give someone ten times more compute or make a thousand copies of them and have those copies work together on a problem. With AI, we can potentially do both.

So once you have a system that can do research at the level of a human AI researcher, you can deploy many instances of that system to improve the next generation. Better systems can then help accelerate that research further. You have this positive feedback loop where progress in AI feeds directly into the process that produces more progress in AI.

That doesn’t mean it’s instantaneous. There may be bottlenecks in compute, experiments, or interacting with the physical world. But I don’t see human-level intelligence as a particularly stable stopping point. It’s a meaningful milestone to us, but there’s no obvious reason that the same process that gets us there would suddenly stop there.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level AI could be deployed in many instances to improve the next generation, creating a positive feedback loop that accelerates AI research, and identifies compute as a possible scaling factor.
